introduction.p: Parametric and polar formulas depend on how a curve is traced. Repeated traversal can multiply a length or area integral, a zero coordinate derivative can invalidate a slope quotient, and signed radii affect the interpretation of polar coordinates. Check the parameter interval before applying a formula.

note.title: A zero velocity may be a feature of the parametrization, not a feature of the curve
note.p: the moving point stops at t=t_0. The curve may still be smooth. The tangent must be found by looking nearby, not by substituting into the slope quotient.

subsection.p: A parametrization is a schedule. A bad or unusual schedule can pause on an otherwise ordinary road.

exercise.title: Why can a parametrization stop even when the curve continues?

statement.p: If both coordinate derivatives vanish, the moving point has zero velocity. In your own words, why might that pause be a feature of the schedule rather than a corner of the geometric curve, and how should the tangent then be found?

hint.p: Look nearby instead of substituting into the slope quotient. A traveler can rest on an otherwise smooth road.

subsection.title: A polar curve traced twice
subsection.p: Polar coordinates have another kind of trap. The same point can have many polar names.
Because of this, a polar equation may trace a geometric curve more than once.
Thus the curve is the circle centered at (1,0) with radius 1.
the circle is traced twice. The second half is not a new region. It is the same circle again, because r becomes negative and the points are plotted in the opposite direction.

subsection.p: The square r^2 makes negative r look harmless algebraically. But negative r can still change the tracing.

exercise.title: Why can a polar area integral count a region twice?

statement.p: The circle r=2\cos\theta is traced twice on [0,2\pi]. In your own words, why does \frac12\int r^2\,d\theta then double the geometric area, and what question should you ask about the interval of \theta before integrating?

hint.p: The formula counts how the polar curve is traced. Choose an interval that sweeps the region exactly once.

warning.title: The 0/0 tangent warning
warning.p: When both coordinate derivatives vanish, the slope formula does not decide the tangent.
Look at the nearby slopes, eliminate the parameter if possible, or study the local geometry.

exercise.title: Why does a 0/0 slope formula fail to decide the tangent?

statement.p: When both parametric derivatives vanish, the slope quotient is undefined. The same issue occurs for polar curves. Describe the different tangent behaviors that can occur and the limits or expansions that can distinguish them.

hint.p: A cusp, a smooth pause, or a retracing may all produce vanishing derivatives. Nearby slopes, elimination of the parameter, or a local picture can tell them apart.

subsection.title: The chapter’s main cautions
subsection.p: The formulas in this chapter are reliable when their hypotheses match the tracing.

cell.p: Is dx/dt\neq0? If both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish, study nearby motion.
Does the parametrization retrace the curve? The length integral counts distance traveled.
Is the curve traced once? What is the orientation?
What interval of \theta sweeps the region exactly once? Does r become negative?

subsection.p: A formula is a tool, not a substitute for the picture.

exercise.title: What habit protects every formula in this chapter?

statement.p: Parametric, polar, and complex languages all carry more information than a plain Cartesian equation. In your own words, why is ask how the curve is being traced the safest habit before using a length, area, or tangent formula?

hint.p: Extra information about direction, speed, and repeated tracing is useful only if you remember that the formula follows the tracing, not just the set of points.
